title: Normal Varieties Normalization and Zariskis Main Theorem

items.title: Local algebra tools for elementary etale changes of classical varieties
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Assume AC and fix an algebraically closed field $k$. For this local packet, an **elementary etale change** is a map of classical affine varieties induced by a finite-type $k$-algebra map locally having a standard smooth presentation with equally many equations and variables and an invertible full Jacobian determinant, together with a chosen point over a given point. The chosen residue fields are both $k$. Such changes are flat, open, and stable under composition, base change, and open restriction. Locally at every classical point their algebra has the form $(A[T]/(P))_h$, with $P$ monic and $P'$ invertible. Their fibres are finite and geometrically reduced. Base change of a reduced finite-type $k$-algebra by such a change is reduced. For a local ring map $A_{\mathfrak m}\to E_{\mathfrak n}$ at a selected point the map is faithfully flat.
items.strategy: direct

references.title: Stacks Project, standard etale local form, Proposition 10.144.4
Stacks Project, flat morphisms locally of finite presentation are open

items.title: Finite relative integral-closure charts for classical quasi-finite morphisms
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Assume AC and let $k$ be algebraically closed. Let $f:X\to Y$ be a separated finite-type morphism of classical varieties with finite fibres, allowing reduced reducible or empty varieties. On an affine open $U$ with coordinate ring $A$, set $M_U=\Gamma(f^{-1}U,\mathcal O_X)$ and $C_U=\operatorname{Int}_A(M_U)$, the integral closure of the image of $A$ in $M_U$. Then $C_U$ is a finite reduced $A$-algebra and $$ (C_U)_a=C_{D(a)} $$ for every $a\in A$. These finite affine spaces glue canonically to a finite classical variety $N\to Y$, and evaluation gives a canonical map $j:X\to N$ over $Y$. Moreover for a flat finite-type $A$-algebra $E$, the sections of the base-changed inverse image are $E\otimes_A M_U$. No assertion that $j$ is an open immersion is made here.
items.strategy: direct

references.title: Stacks Project, relative normalization
Stacks Project, flat base change for structure sheaf sections
Stacks Project, polynomial algebras over fields have finite integral closures

items.title: Relative integral closure under elementary etale change
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Assume AC and let $A$ be a reduced finite-type algebra over an algebraically closed field $k$. Let $A\to B$ be any algebra map and $C=\operatorname{Int}_A(B)\subseteq B$. If $A\to E$ is an elementary etale algebra change as constructed in [[lem-av7-zero-dimensional-standard-smooth-local-tools]], then $$E\otimes_A C\;=\;\operatorname{Int}_E(E\otimes_A B)$$ inside $E\otimes_A B$. Injectivity on the left is part of the assertion. The algebra $B$ need not be finite type, reduced, or a domain.
items.strategy: direct

references.title: Stacks Project, integral closure and etale extension, Lemmas 10.147.1 and 10.147.2

items.title: Finite fibre components after an elementary etale change
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Assume AC, let $k$ be algebraically closed, and let $f:X\to Y$ be separated and of finite type between classical varieties, with finite fibres. For a point $y\in Y$ and distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in f^{-1}(y)$ there is an elementary etale change $(T,t)\to(Y,y)$ and an open-and-closed decomposition $$ X\times_Y T=W\sqcup V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_n $$ such that each $V_i\to T$ is finite, its fibre over $t$ is the singleton mapping to $x_i$, and $W_t$ contains none of those selected points. Fibres here retain their finite local algebras, not just their reduced point sets. Taking all points of $f^{-1}(y)$ makes $W_t$ empty.
items.strategy: direct

references.title: Stacks Project, coprime polynomial factorization after etale change
Stacks Project, finite components around isolated fibre points
Stacks Project, separated finite-component decomposition

items.title: Classical Zariski Main from relative integral-closure neighbourhoods
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $k$ be algebraically closed. Let $f:X\to Y$ be a **separated morphism of finite type with finite fibres** between classical varieties, allowing reduced reducible or empty varieties. On each affine $U\subseteq Y$, take the integral closure $C_U$ of $k[U]$ in $\Gamma(f^{-1}U,\mathcal O_X)$. The finite affine spaces of these algebras glue to a finite classical morphism $\nu:N\to Y$, and their evaluation maps glue to an open immersion $j:X\hookrightarrow N$ with $f=\nu\circ j$. Thus every separated quasi-finite classical morphism factors as an open immersion followed by a finite morphism. Its finite affine atlas makes both source and target quasi-compact; separatedness gives quasi-separatedness. No quasi-projectivity, normality, separability, or smoothness assumption is added. This item proves the classical finite-type case; it makes no assertion for arbitrary non-Noetherian schemes.
items.strategy: direct

references.title: Stacks Project, nonaffine Zariski Main, Lemmas 37.43.1–37.43.3
Grothendieck and Dieudonne, EGA IV, part 4, 18.12.12–18.12.15

items.title: Proper quasi-finite classical morphisms are finite
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $k$ be algebraically closed. A proper quasi-finite morphism $f:X\to Y$ of classical varieties is finite. Here proper means separated, of finite type, and universally closed; quasi-finite means of finite type with finite fibres. This assertion uses the full separated quasi-finite factorization, not merely its affine-source case. In particular a classical projective morphism with finite fibres is finite.
items.strategy: Use the full separated classical Zariski Main factorization. Universal closedness closes the graph image, giving an open-and-closed finite-model subvariety represented by an idempotent and a finite quotient algebra, including the empty image. For the exact Chevalley projective finite-fiber case, the earlier projective projection closedness theorem applies after each classical base change.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry, Proposition 8.54
The Stacks Project, Lemma 37.44.1

items.title: Finite morphisms over a projective variety over any field
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be any field and let $f:X\to Y$ be a finite morphism of finite-type $k$-schemes: on every affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq Y$, $f^{-1}(U)=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is affine and $B$ is a finite $A$-module. If $Y$ is projective, then $f$ admits a closed immersion $X\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_Y$ over $Y$ for some $N$, and $X$ is projective over $k$.

Every such finite morphism is also separated, of finite type and universally closed. More generally these three properties follow for any finite morphism of finite-type $k$-schemes by the same affine algebra calculation; consequently a finite classical morphism to a complete variety has complete source.

No normality, smoothness, flatness, or separability assumption is needed. The finite algebra $f_*\mathcal O_X$ can fail to be locally free; the projectivization used below is that of a coherent module, not a vector bundle.
items.strategy: Over any field use the finite coherent algebra F=f_*O_X and E=O_Y⊕F. Build projectivization from homogeneous module presentations and affine ratio charts. Homogenized monic equations show the finite evaluation image is a closed scheme with no infinity. Clear denominators and kill overlap differences on the finite standard cover to generate E(m) globally; obtain one closed embedding into P^N_Y and compose with Segre. Finite base change, universal closedness and finite-over-complete are proved by local algebra independently of projectivity.

references.title: The Stacks Project, Lemma 29.45.16, finite morphisms are projective
The Stacks Project, Lemma 29.44.16, projective morphisms over a base with an ample invertible sheaf

items.title: Normal points and normal varieties
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice for affine-coordinate and localization interfaces. A point $x$ of a classical variety $X$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ is normal when its local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is an integrally closed domain. The variety $X$ is normal when every point is normal; equivalently, when $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is integrally closed for every $x\in X$.
items.strategy: Define normality through the published germ/local-ring and normal-Noetherian-ring interfaces, not through an embedding or a chosen affine chart. Record that on a reducible variety a point lying on two components fails to be normal because its local ring is not a domain.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: Normality is checked on affine open charts
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a classical variety over algebraically closed $k$ with a finite affine open cover $X=U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_n$, $U_i$ with coordinate ring $A_i$. Then $X$ is normal if and only if every $A_i$ is an integrally closed domain. A single normal point need only be checked in one affine chart containing it.
items.strategy: For $x\in U_i$ the local ring $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is the localisation of $A_i$ at the corresponding maximal ideal. Use the local criterion for integrally closed domains and the fact that the maximal ideals of the chart meet every point; principal opens are affine so the criterion may be applied on any chart.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
Michael Artin, MIT 18.721 Algebraic Geometry notes (January 26, 2022), Ch. 4

items.title: Regular varieties are normal
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. At every regular point of a classical variety over an algebraically closed field the local ring is an integrally closed domain; hence every regular variety is normal. No characteristic or perfectness hypothesis is needed.
items.strategy: Unfold regularity geometrically as the published local-ring condition and apply the commutative-algebra theorem that regular local rings are integrally closed domains. No Jacobian computation is re-proved here.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: A normal variety is regular in codimension one
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a normal classical variety over an algebraically closed field and let $x\in X$ be a point whose local ring has dimension one, equivalently a codimension-one point of an irreducible component. Then $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is a discrete valuation ring; in particular $x$ is a regular point of $X$. The statement holds in every characteristic and does not need $X$ to be irreducible.
items.strategy: Localise to an affine chart and apply the theorem that height-one localisations of normal Noetherian domains are discrete valuation rings; the DVR characterisation in dimension one turns this into regularity. Dimension one of the local ring is the codimension-one condition.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: The normalization of an irreducible affine variety
items.strategy: Use the object-level algebra-variety dictionary to realise $B$ by an affine variety; well-definedness uses finiteness of the integral closure over a finite-type domain over a field and closedness of the integral closure. The morphism is the one induced by the inclusion through the coordinate-ring anti-equivalence. Uniqueness is recorded again in the corollary below.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
The Stacks Project, Section 29.55 Normalization (Definition 29.55.1, Lemmas 29.55.2-29.55.3)
references.locator: Chapter 29 Morphisms, Section 29.55, Definition 29.55.1 and Lemmas 29.55.2-29.55.3

items.title: The affine normalization is finite, birational, and surjective
items.strategy: Finiteness and normality of $X^{\nu}$ are the published affine-normalization corollary. Surjectivity is lying over for the integral inclusion $A\hookrightarrow B$. Birationality is the identity $\operatorname{Frac}(B)=k(X)$, converted into an isomorphism of function fields and then into a dominant birational correspondence via the function-field dictionary.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: The normalization is an isomorphism over the normal locus
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be an irreducible affine variety with normalization $
u:X^{
u}	o X$. The normal locus of $X$ is a dense open subset, and at every normal point $x$ there is a principal open $D(f)
i x$ with $A_f$ integrally closed; on $
u^{-1}(D(f))$ the map $
u$ restricts to an isomorphism onto $D(f)$. Consequently $
u$ is an isomorphism over the normal locus.
items.strategy: At a normal point $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is integrally closed, and $B/A$ is a finite module, so a finite set of denominators clears the discrepancy: some $f$ with $x\in D(f)$ satisfies $A_f=B_f$. Finiteness of $B/A$ makes the vanishing condition localisable, and principal opens are affine; the restriction statement follows from localization compatibility of the normalization.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
Ravi Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry (November 18, 2017 public draft), §9.7 and §29.6

items.title: Normalization of a classical variety by gluing affine normalizations
items.strategy: Choose a finite affine cover and normalise each chart; the common function field makes the chart normalizations canonically comparable. On overlaps use finite principal-open refinements and localization compatibility to identify the two models inside the common function field, check the cocycle condition, and glue the varieties, their structure sheaves, and the projections. Finiteness is affine-local by its defining finite-module charts, and the resulting morphism is birational and surjective because it is so on every chart.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
Michael Artin, MIT 18.721 Algebraic Geometry notes (January 26, 2022), Ch. 4 §§4.2-4.3 (Integral extensions; Normalization)

items.title: Universal property of the normalization
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be an irreducible classical variety over an
algebraically closed field with normalization $\nu\colon X^{\nu}\to X$. If
$f\colon Y\to X$ is a dominant birational morphism from a normal variety $Y$,
then there is a unique morphism $g\colon Y\to X^{\nu}$ with $\nu\circ g=f$. In
the affine case the corresponding ring statement is: if
$A\subseteq B\subseteq\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ with $B$ integrally closed, then
the integral closure of $A$ lies in $B$.
items.strategy: In each affine chart the pullback is an inclusion $A\hookrightarrow B$ of domains with a common fraction field, and the integral closure $A'$ of $A$ is contained in every integrally closed intermediate ring, so $A'\subseteq B$ and the ring map $A'\to B$ exists. The chartwise maps agree on overlaps because they are determined by the common function field, so they glue; uniqueness follows by agreeing on the dense open over which $\nu$ is an isomorphism and applying the equality-on-dense-open lemma.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8 §a-b: the universal property of the normalization
The Stacks Project, Lemma 29.55.5 (normalization and its universal property)

items.title: The normalization is unique up to unique isomorphism
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a classical variety over an algebraically closed field and let $\nu_i:X_i\to X$, $i=1,2$, be normalizations. There is a unique isomorphism $X_1\xrightarrow{\sim}X_2$ over $X$.
items.strategy: Apply the universal property to each normalizing morphism in turn to obtain maps in both directions over $X$; the composites are maps over $X$ between normalizations and are unique with that property, hence are the identities. No choice beyond the universal property and the finiteness of the maps is used.

items.title: Normalization commutes with restriction to an open subvariety
items.strategy: Principal opens are affine, and the affine normalization of $A_f$ is the localisation $B_f$ inside the common function field. Cover $U$ by principal opens of an affine cover and glue; normality restricts to open subvarieties and finiteness is affine-local.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
Ravi Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry (November 18, 2017 public draft), §9.7 and §29.6

items.title: Unibranch points of a classical variety
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A point $x$ of a classical variety $X$ is unibranch when its fibre $\nu^{-1}(x)$ under the normalization is a single point, with one analytic branch in the curve case. Every normal point is unibranch, since the normalization is an isomorphism near it; the converse fails, as the cusp shows. Unibranchness is a property of the point alone and does not require $X$ to be irreducible only through the component containing $x$.
items.strategy: Define the property through the canonical normalization morphism and its finite fibres. Normality implies unibranch by the isomorphism-over-the-normal-locus lemma; the failure of the converse is recorded by the cusp example on the companion page and is not used as a proof here.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
Ravi Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry (November 18, 2017 public draft), §9.7 and §29.6

items.title: A normal curve over a perfect field is nonsingular
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be an integral separated finite-type $k$-scheme of
dimension one over a perfect field $k$ (in particular a classical curve when
$k$ is algebraically closed). Then $X$ is normal if and only if $X$
is regular, and over a perfect field this is equivalent to $X$ being
nonsingular (smooth over $k$). The perfectness hypothesis cannot be dropped for
the smooth equivalence.
items.strategy: Treat integral finite-type scheme curves over any perfect field: the generic stalk is a regular field and every nongeneric normal stalk is a one-dimensional Noetherian domain, hence a DVR. Prove the normal/regular directions separately, then apply the earlier arbitrary finite-type perfect-field smoothness criterion. The explicit purely inseparable curve Spec(F_p(s^(1/p))[t]) is normal and regular but has a nonregular scalar-extension stalk, proving perfectness necessary for smoothness.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8 §a-b: normal points and curves (Definition 8.1 and the DVR characterisation of one-dimensional normal local rings)

items.title: Normalization resolves the singularities of a projective curve
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $C$ be an irreducible projective curve over a
perfect field $k$. Then its normalization $C^{\nu}$ is a nonsingular projective
curve, and $\nu\colon C^{\nu}\to C$ is a finite birational morphism.
Consequently every irreducible projective curve over a perfect field admits a
nonsingular projective model.
items.strategy: Inside the common function field normalize the standard projective affine charts using the earlier all-field finite integral-closure theorem. Principal localization identifies overlaps, so the affine schemes glue into the finite birational normal curve; clear denominators for the dense isomorphism and use transcendence degree for dimension one. The generalized finite-over-projective helper supplies one global projective embedding, and the perfect-field normal-curve theorem supplies smoothness.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8 §b: normalization of curves and nonsingular projective models

items.title: Finite morphisms of classical varieties
items.statement: A morphism $f:X\to Y$ of classical varieties is finite when for every affine open $U\subseteq Y$ the inverse image $f^{-1}(U)$ is affine and its coordinate ring is a finite module over $k[U]$ along $f^{*}$. It suffices to test this on the members of one finite affine cover of $Y$ by principal opens. Finiteness is affine-local on the target and is preserved by restriction to open subvarieties of $Y$.
items.strategy: Define finiteness by the finite-module condition on coordinate rings in affine charts, using the coordinate-ring anti-equivalence to state the condition intrinsically. Record the affine-local character of the definition as part of the item, since later proofs reduce to an affine cover by the Noetherian-components lemma.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: Finite morphisms are closed with finite fibres
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. A finite morphism $f:X\to Y$ of classical varieties over an algebraically closed field is closed, and every fibre $f^{-1}(y)$ is a finite set. The statement holds in every characteristic and needs no flatness, separability, or normality hypothesis.
items.strategy: Reduce to an affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}(B)\to\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ with $B$ a finite $A$-module. For a closed subset $V(J)\subseteq X$, the image is $V(J\cap A)$: lying over and going up give the two inclusions using the integrality of $A\to B$. For the fibre over a closed point $\mathfrak m$, the fibre ring $B/\mathfrak mB$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra, hence Artinian, and has only finitely many maximal ideals, which are exactly the points of the fibre by the Nullstellensatz dictionary.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: A finite birational morphism onto a normal variety is an isomorphism
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:Y\to X$ be a finite birational morphism of classical varieties over an algebraically closed field. If $X$ is normal, then $f$ is an isomorphism. The normality of the target is essential: the normalization of the cusp is finite and birational but not an isomorphism.
items.strategy: On affine charts, $A\subseteq B$ with $B$ a finite $A$-module and $\operatorname{Frac}(B)=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. Normality of $X$ makes $A$ integrally closed; every element of $B$ is integral over $A$ by module finiteness, hence lies in $A$. Thus $A=B$ on every chart and the morphisms agree with the chartwise identities.

references.title: The Stacks Project, Lemma 29.55.8 (finite birational morphisms onto normal schemes are isomorphisms)
references.locator: Chapter 29 Morphisms, Section 29.55, Lemma 29.55.8 and its proof

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: Zariski's Main Theorem: open immersion followed by a finite morphism
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f:X\to Y$ be a separated morphism of finite type with finite fibres (quasi-finite in the classical sense) between classical varieties over an algebraically closed field. Then $f$ factors as $f=\nu\circ j$ with $j:X\hookrightarrow N$ an open immersion and $\nu:N\to Y$ finite. This is the exact classical form of Zariski's Main Theorem used by the later items of this page.
items.strategy: Quote the proved local bridge for the separated quasi-finite classical factorization and repackage it in the page's finite-morphism register, recording the full hypotheses (separated, finite type, finite fibres) and the AC cost. The bridge already constructs the relative integral closure model, glues it, and proves the open-immersion property.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
The Stacks Project, Section 37.43 Zariski's Main Theorem (Lemmas 37.43.1-37.43.3)
references.locator: Chapter 37 More on Morphisms, Section 37.43, Lemmas 37.43.1-37.43.3 and their proofs

references.title: Ravi Vakil, The Rising Sea: Foundations of Algebraic Geometry (November 18, 2017 public draft), §9.7 and §29.6
Grothendieck and Dieudonne, EGA IV, part 4 (Publications mathematiques de l'IHES 32), §18.12.12-18.12.15

items.title: Birational quasi-finite maps to normal targets are open immersions
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f\colon Y\to X$ be a finite morphism of
classical varieties over an algebraically closed field. If $f$ is birational
and $X$ is normal, then $f$ is an isomorphism. In particular bijectivity plus
finiteness does not repair a failure of normality of the target, as the cusp
example on the companion page shows.

More generally, a quasi-finite birational morphism $f:Y\to X$ of irreducible classical varieties with normal target $X$ is an open immersion. If it is bijective, it is an isomorphism even without an additional finiteness hypothesis.
items.strategy: Retain the finite birational normal-target isomorphism case. For quasi-finite birational maps apply the fully proved local classical Zariski Main theorem, take the reduced irreducible closure of the open source inside its finite model, and observe that its affine algebras remain finite quotient modules. The restricted finite map is birational to the normal target, hence isomorphic; therefore the source is open, and bijectivity makes that open equal the target.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8 §a and §c: finite birational maps onto normal varieties

items.title: Regular functions on a normal variety are determined in codimension one
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a normal classical variety over an algebraically closed field, with function field $k(X)$, and let $\varphi\in k(X)$ be a rational function. Then $\varphi$ is regular on all of $X$ if and only if $\varphi\in\mathcal O_{X,x}$ at every codimension-one point $x\in X$. Equivalently, the regular functions on $X$ are exactly the intersection, inside $k(X)$, of the local rings at the codimension-one points.
items.strategy: On an affine chart the statement is the commutative-algebra description of a normal Noetherian domain as the intersection of its height-one localisations, which holds for normal domains by Serre's criterion and the membership lemma. Passing between charts is legitimate because the function field is common and regularity is local; each local ring at a codimension-one point is a DVR by the preceding theorem.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
Michael Artin, MIT 18.721 Algebraic Geometry notes (January 26, 2022), Ch. 4

items.title: A rational function with no codimension-one poles is regular
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a normal classical variety and $\varphi\in k(X)$. If $\varphi$ is regular at every codimension-one point of $X$, then $\varphi$ is a global regular function on $X$.
items.strategy: This is the forward direction of the codimension-one intersection theorem; no additional hypothesis is used, and the corollary is the form in which the result is applied to extend functions across normal varieties.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: The conductor of a normalization
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\nu:X^{\nu}\to X$ be the normalization of an irreducible classical variety. On a nonempty affine chart U with coordinate ring A and normalization preimage with coordinate ring B, the conductor is $\mathfrak c_U=\operatorname{Ann}_A(B/A)=\{a\in A:aB\subseteq A\}$. On D(f) with f nonzero, the normalization has coordinate ring B_f, the integral closure of A_f inside k(X), and the conductor is (c_U)_f. For f=0 the open is empty and the localized rings and ideals are zero, with no field-closure assertion. These ideals glue to an ideal sheaf c in O_X; the support of O_X/c, equivalently V(c), is exactly the nonnormal locus where the normalization fails to be an isomorphism.
items.strategy: Define the conductor chartwise as the annihilator of the finite module $B/A$ and prove compatibility with principal localisation so that the chartwise ideals agree on overlaps. The support statement uses the isomorphism-over-the-normal-locus lemma and the finite-module support interface.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: The conductor is an ideal of both the coordinate ring and its normalization
items.statement: Let $A\subseteq B$ be an inclusion of domains with $B$ the normalization of $A$ in a common fraction field. The conductor $\mathfrak c=\operatorname{Ann}_A(B/A)$ is an ideal of $A$ and also an ideal of $B$: for $a\in\mathfrak c$ and $b\in B$ one has $ab\in\mathfrak c$. Consequently $\mathfrak c=\mathfrak c B$ generates the same ideal in $B$, and the quotient $B/\mathfrak c$ is a finite $k$-vector space in the geometric setting.
items.strategy: Verify the colon calculation directly: $aB\subseteq A$ implies $(ab)B\subseteq aB\subseteq A$, so $ab\in\mathfrak c$; the ideal axioms in $A$ follow from the annihilator interface. Finiteness of $B/A$ over $A$ makes the quotient finite-dimensional over $k$.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: Normalization need not resolve singularities in dimension at least two
items.statement: For curves over a perfect field normalization removes all singularities, but in dimension at least two a normal variety can still be singular: the quadric cone $xy=z^2$ is normal with an isolated singular point. Normalization therefore only removes the non-normal locus, not the singular locus, and the theory of resolution of singularities is a separate subject.
items.strategy: Record the counterexample on the companion page and cite the normality of a hypersurface with an isolated singularity. No proof is asserted here; the remark isolates the boundary of the curve theorem.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8 Summary 8.13 and Aside 9.39: the cone z^2 = xy is normal but not factorial, hence normal with an isolated singularity

title: Normal Varieties Normalization and Zariskis Main Theorem — Examples

items.title: Normalizing the cuspidal plane curve
items.statement: Let $X=V(y^2-x^3)\subseteq\mathbf A^2$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic not two. The normalization of $X$ is $\mathbf A^1\to X$, $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$, with coordinate ring inclusion $k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)\cong k[t^2,t^3]\hookrightarrow k[t]$. The map is finite and birational, the cusp is the unique non-normal point, its fibre is a single point, and the conductor of the extension is the maximal ideal $(t^2,t^3)$ of $k[t^2,t^3]$.
items.strategy: Compute the integral closure of $k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3)$ in its fraction field as $k[t]$ and identify the normalization morphism through the coordinate-ring anti-equivalence. The fibre over the cusp is computed from the local ring, and the conductor from the colon ideal $\{a: a\cdot k[t]\subseteq k[t^2,t^3]\}$.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: Normalizing the nodal plane curve
items.statement: Let $X=V(y^2-x^2(x+1))\subseteq\mathbf A^2$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic not two. Its normalization is $\mathbf A^1\to X$, $t\mapsto(t^2-1,t(t^2-1))$, a finite birational map whose fibre over the node consists of the two points $t=\pm1$. The node is not unibranch, so it is not normal.
items.strategy: Parametrise the nodal curve by the lines through the node and identify the inverse map on the punctured curve; the two branches correspond to the two tangent directions. Compute the fibre over the node from the two local branches and record that the normalization separates them.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: Affine space is normal
items.statement: Affine $n$-space $\mathbf A^n_k$ over an algebraically closed field is normal: its coordinate ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is an integrally closed domain, so every local ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]_{\mathfrak m}$ is integrally closed as well.
items.strategy: The polynomial ring is integrally closed in its fraction field by the published polynomial-closure theorem, and normality of a domain is local by the published normality-locality theorem; every local ring of affine space is the localisation of the polynomial ring at a maximal ideal.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: Normalization of the node is two-to-one over the node
items.statement: The normalization map of the nodal curve is not injective: the node has two preimages under the normalization. Hence a normalization can never be assumed injective in dimension one, in contrast with the normal case where it is an isomorphism.
items.strategy: Use the computed normalization of the node and evaluate at the two parameters mapping to the node; the fibre is a two-point set, so the map fails injectivity. This refutes the general claim that normalization is injective.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: A normal singular surface: the quadric cone
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic not two, the quadric cone $X=V(xy-z^2)\subseteq\mathbf A^3$ is normal but singular at the origin. Hence normal does not imply smooth in dimension two.
items.strategy: The cone is a hypersurface and the Jacobian ideal of $xy-z^2$ is $(y,x,-2z)=(x,y,z)$, so the singular locus is the origin. Serre's criterion applies: the ring is regular in codimension one because every height-one localisation localises from a smooth closed point, and it satisfies $S_2$ because $(x,y)$ is a regular sequence of length two at the origin while all other local rings are regular and hence Cohen-Macaulay. The ring is a domain by irreducibility of $xy-z^2$ and the Nullstellensatz correspondence, and a normal domain by the criterion.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: The cusp normalization is bijective but not an isomorphism
items.statement: The normalization of the cusp is finite and bijective onto the cusp but is not an isomorphism; the failure is exactly that the target cusp is not normal. This shows the normality hypothesis in the finite-birational-isomorphism lemma cannot be replaced by bijectivity.
items.strategy: The normalization of the cusp is bijective because the cusp has a single branch and its normalization is $\mathbf A^1$ with the cusp as image; it is not an isomorphism because the pullback map on coordinate rings $k[t^2,t^3]\hookrightarrow k[t]$ is not surjective. The target fails to be normal at the cusp.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: The conductor of the cusp is generated by the gap exponents
items.statement: For the cusp $k[t^2,t^3]\subseteq k[t]$, the conductor is the ideal $(t^2,t^3)$ of $k[t^2,t^3]$: the least exponent $m$ such that $t^n\in k[t^2,t^3]$ for every $n\ge m$ is $m=2$, and $t^2$ does not generate the conductor alone since $t^3$ is not a multiple of $t^2$ inside the semigroup ring.
items.strategy: Compute the colon ideal directly: $a=t^2$ and $a=t^3$ multiply $k[t]$ into $k[t^2,t^3]$, and no smaller-degree monomial does; the semigroup generated by $2$ and $3$ contains every integer $\ge2$ except $3$ is in fact present, so the conductor is $(t^2,t^3)$ and the least exponent from which all monomials lie in the semigroup is $2$.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8

items.title: Finite fibres do not make an open immersion finite
items.statement: The inclusion $j:\mathbf A^1\setminus\{0\}\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^1$ is a quasi-finite open immersion with finite fibres, but it is not finite: the coordinate ring inclusion $k[t]\hookrightarrow k[t,t^{-1}]$ is not module-finite, and finite morphisms are closed whereas the image of $j$ is not closed. Thus quasi-finiteness plus open immersion does not imply finiteness; the missing hypothesis is properness.
items.strategy: Show $k[t,t^{-1}]$ is not a finite $k[t]$-module because the powers $t^{-n}$ generate an infinite strictly decreasing chain of submodules, and cite the theorem that finite morphisms are closed to see that the non-closed image of $j$ excludes finiteness. The example is the standard witness that the properness half of Zariski's Main Theorem is needed.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Algebraic Geometry (2025 version), Ch. 8
